description: A team of two working on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge.
summary:
Is that dot moving, and what is it? Ephemerix answers that for any position or name you type. It blinks 16 years of NASA infrared images, WISE and NEOWISE from 2010 to 2024 then SPHEREx, on one grid; measures how fast the object moves beside the published value; and reads its SPHEREx spectrum where the object was on each date to give a type, or says why it cannot. Simple mode gives a large blink and a two-sentence answer; Advanced shows every measurement.

It does what the brief asks: coordinates in, a video out, all 102 SPHEREx bands, Gaia and WISE overlays, and checks on the brief's five targets. On those and twelve brown dwarfs, 14 of 16 measured motions agree with the catalogue; the 2 that do not are shown with their reasons.

It matters because most known brown dwarfs were found by volunteers comparing images, and no one person can sift all that data. Anyone can check a dot in a minute or two and post the evidence to Backyard Worlds. When a public archive is down, as IRSA was during the event, it keeps working where it can and says what is missing and why.
details:
Is that dot moving, and what is it?

Ephemerix blinks 16 years of infrared sky for any position you type and shows its measured motion next to the published one: 14 of 16 agree, and the 2 that do not are on the page.One screen, one answer: 16 years of WISE and SPHEREx images of 2MASS J0415-0935, its measured motion beside the catalogue's, and the type read from its SPHEREx spectrum beside the published one.

Check it in two minutes

  • WISE 0855-0714 in Simple mode: https://ephemerix.vercel.app/?target=wise-0855-0714&mode=simple. One of the coldest brown dwarfs known, moving 8.16 arcsec a year against the catalogue's 8.15.
  • Every check against published values, failures included: https://ephemerix.vercel.app/validation.html
  • The sky map, to open any prepared view: https://ephemerix.vercel.app/explore.html

Source code (MIT licence): https://github.com/Unluckyathecking/Ephemerix

What it does and how it works

You type a position or a name. The search box takes coordinates in any common format, in degrees or hours, such as the brief's 08h55m10.831s, -7d14m42.53s. Names are suggested as you type from the site's own list of 53 SIMBAD objects with their positions and motions; any other name goes to CDS Sesame, and a Solar System body to JPL's Small-Body Database, with its position from JPL Horizons.

The view is then built from WISE and NEOWISE images from 2010 to 2024 and SPHEREx images from 2025 on, from NASA's IRSA archive or its public cloud copies, all resampled to one grid and played in date order.

  • Motion. The object's motion is fitted from its positions across the images and compared with the catalogue's.
  • Spectrum. Each SPHEREx exposure is read at the object's own position on that exposure's date, because a nearby object moves: WISE 0855-0714 crosses more than one 6.15 arcsec SPHEREx pixel a year. The spectrum is compared with brown-dwarf templates; when the data cannot support a type, none is given and the page says why.
  • What else moved. Every WISE visit of the patch is searched blind for anything else that moved, then searched again with the visit dates shuffled, when nothing real can line up, to measure false alarms.

The SPHEREx spectrum of 2MASS J0415-0935 with the best brown-dwarf template over it: dark where methane and water absorb, bright near 4 microns, typed T7 to T9 against a published T8.

What benefits it has

  • A Backyard Worlds volunteer checking whether a moving dot is real gets the evidence behind one link and a ready-to-post summary for Talk.
  • Students and the curious get Simple mode: a large blink, a two-sentence answer and "What am I looking at?".
  • Astronomers get Advanced mode: every measurement, band, overlay and data-quality note behind the answer.

It covers what the brief asked for: coordinates in the URL, all 102 SPHEREx bands with a methane false-colour view, a field of view from 2 to 8 arcmin, the difference or sum of two dates, Gaia and CatWISE overlays, embedding, plain-word contamination notes, and a footer naming the SPHEREx data in use.

What impact we intend

The brief notes that most known brown dwarfs "were discovered by volunteers" comparing images taken at different times, and that "no one person can sift through all that data alone". We want anyone to check one dot against 16 years of data in a minute or two, see how sure the answer is, and share it; the archive status record is for anyone building on these archives.

What tools, languages and services we used

  • Python with Astropy, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, PyVO and FastAPI for the measurements and the live lookup service, which runs on Modal.
  • Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Plotly.js for the site, on Vercel, with no build step and nothing loaded from other hosts.
  • Our own index of 1,628,229 SPHEREx frames, which finds the frames over a position in about 5 ms against 3 to 5 s from the archive's search.

How it is creative

Simple and Advanced. Our first version was dense, as tools made for astronomers tend to be; our test was whether someone who has never seen an infrared image could get the answer. One switch at the top of every page changes the whole site, and a link keeps its mode.

Any position, live. A volunteer's new candidate is by definition in nobody's prepared gallery, so anything beyond the 19 prepared views is built on request from the public archives. In one run Luhman 16, with no prepared view, took 82 s.

The sky map. Most people do not carry coordinates in their head. The map is 8,876 Hipparcos stars you can drag and zoom, with our views and nearby known objects marked. Tap one to open it, or press "Take me to something that moves"; "Back to the sky map" returns you where you left off.

Archive uptime. Most web services have an independent status page; for the astronomy archives a tool like this depends on, we found no such browsable record, so we built one. Every 5 minutes our server asks each of the nine services it uses one light question and keeps 30 days of answers. A row of marks by the search box shows which are answering now; the status page opens any day, then any hour, down to each check; and a view that is missing something names the archive that did not answer.The archive status page: one block per day for 30 days, then each hour and each check, for the nine services the search depends on.

What factors we considered

The archives can fail. They did, on and off, during the event. On 14 and 15 November nine threads on the Space Apps discussion board reported IRSA returning errors or down (#2183, #2208, #2218, #2224, #2237, #2245, #2249, #2257, #2285); the organisers acknowledged in #2224 that "some parts of the IRSA website are experiencing difficulties". Our status checks on 15 November, from 18:32 to 19:37 GMT, found NASA IRSA's image search answering none of 14. When the image search is down, WISE frames are read from the public cloud copy instead: at 19:41 GMT on 15 November, with IRSA's image search and ESA's Gaia archive both not answering, a live lookup of Betelgeuse still returned 46 WISE and 18 SPHEREx images and said its star markers were missing because Gaia was down.

A wrong answer is worse than none. For someone about to post a candidate, a wrong type does harm, so a type is withheld with its reason, and the blind search reports how often it cries wolf.WISE 0855-0714: the motion agrees with the catalogue, but a star shares the SPHEREx pixel, so the spectrum is left unclassified and the page says why.

How well it works

We tested 17 objects with published types and motions: the brief's five (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis), seven Backyard Worlds brown dwarfs and five benchmarks. A motion agrees when both components are within 3 sigma of our fit error.

  • Motion: 14 of 16 measured agree and 2 differ; CWISE J2021+1524 was not detected. For R Draconis and RW Aurigae, which barely move, agreement only shows we measure no false motion.
  • Type: 8 of 8 types contain the published type, 2 of them provisional because a neighbour may add light; one more, faint and open-ended, is counted apart. 6 are unclassified, each with its reason.
  • What else moved: the target found again in 11 of 17 fields, with no unexplained tracks; beside CWISE J2029-7910 it re-found the target's known host star, 34 arcsec away and moving with it, a known pair recovered, not a discovery.
  • The two motions that differ: Epsilon Indi B is an unresolved pair; for CWISE J1055+5443, fitting a neighbour removed about 10 of an original 40 mas/yr miss, and the rest is not explained.
  • Variable stars: R Draconis saturates, so its brightness is measured from the unsaturated ring around the centre against comparison stars measured the same way, a form of the wing photometry that a navigator's reply on the Space Apps discussion board called "optional extra credit" (#2282). The page gives relative brightness only, states the method, and says which bands held against tests written beforehand.

Every check against published values, failures included: the scoreboard is computed from the same data file as the tables under it.

Planet X. It is predicted at 400 to 800 au; one SPHEREx map reaches a 10-Earth-mass planet to about 375 au, and our pilot search is far too shallow, so we claim no Planet X.Could SPHEREx see Planet X? Predicted brightness of each hypothetical planet against distance, with the depth of each survey: at 400 to 800 au it falls below one SPHEREx map.

What did not work, and limits

  • A learned vetting classifier lost to a plain S/N cut and is not used; a denoising filter failed a pass mark set in advance and is not used.
  • Types are a guide, given as a range one to two subtypes either side, tested from L1 to Y0.
  • Some thresholds were set after we saw results; the results page lists each, with its effect.
  • We have not timed Ephemerix against volunteers.

Use of AI

Before the event I used Claude to research the challenge and the SPHEREx and WISE archives and to brainstorm approaches, and I chose the direction from that. No project code was written before the hackathon began. During the event, AI agents wrote most of the code and ran the measurement campaigns under my direction. I set the goals and made the product decisions, and I decided what was good enough to publish.

No AI-generated images, audio or video are used.
